name: Trofinetide (investigational uses)
route: Tested as an IV infusion (brain injury) and as an oral liquid (fragile X)
status: Approved only for Rett syndrome (Daybue); brain injury, concussion and fragile X programs stalled, with no active trials
mechanism: A stabilized copy of GPE, an IGF-1 fragment that limited inflammation and nerve-cell death after brain injury in animal studies

article.summary: Before trofinetide was approved for Rett syndrome, it was tested for brain injury, concussion and fragile X syndrome. Those programs stalled, and none is active in 2026.
article.takeaway: Trofinetide started life as a brain-protection drug: a stabilized copy of GPE, a tiny fragment of IGF-1 that limited damage in animal models of stroke and brain injury.[^1][^2] Given by IV infusion to about 260 people with moderate to severe traumatic brain injury, in a trial run with the US Army, it was safe but did not beat placebo on recovery measures.[^3][^4] A small oral study in males with fragile X syndrome showed encouraging signals at the higher dose,[^5] but development focused on Rett syndrome, where it was approved in 2023 as [Daybue](/peptides/trofinetide). As of October 2026, no trials outside Rett syndrome are active.
glance: Investigational outside Rett syndrome; programs inactive
Moderate to severe brain injury, concussion, fragile X syndrome
72-hour IV infusion after brain injury; twice-daily liquid in fragile X
Two phase 2 brain injury trials, one phase 2 fragile X trial, many animal studies

blocks.text: IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) protects nerve cells and improves recovery after brain injury in animals, but as a large protein it enters the brain poorly and can spur unwanted cell growth. In the brain, enzymes clip off its first three amino acids, glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), and that small fragment turned out to be protective on its own in ischemic injury models.[^1]

Natural GPE breaks down quickly and had to be infused continuously. Trofinetide adds a methyl group to the proline, which lengthened its half-life and allowed oral use. In rats it shrank stroke damage and reduced brain inflammation and inflammatory signaling after a penetrating, ballistic-like brain injury.[^2][^6]

rows: 72-hour IV infusion started within 7 hours of injury, about 260 men
Safe, but no benefit on main recovery measures (reported 2016)[^3][^4]
Oral treatment, 32 people at one US Army site
Oral liquid, 72 adolescent and adult males, 28 days
Higher dose met prespecified success criteria[^5]

blocks.text: The brain injury trial, called INTREPID2566, enrolled men aged 18-70 with Glasgow Coma Scale scores of 4-12, randomized to placebo or one of three infusion rates.[^3] Neuren, the developer, reported no drug-related safety trends but no difference from placebo on a functional outcome scale, a disability inventory or deaths. An exploratory cognitive test battery favored the drug. The company pointed to more severely injured patients than expected, uneven randomization and drug levels as possible reasons.[^4]

Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. In a four-week exploratory trial, the 70 mg/kg twice-daily dose met a prespecified composite definition of success, and the group improved on three fragile X-specific measures.[^5] The study was small and short, and no larger confirmatory trial has followed.

At the doses used in these programs, trofinetide was generally well tolerated: both fragile X doses were judged safe,[^5] and the brain injury trial found no dose-related trends in side effects or lab results.[^4] The much higher oral doses later used in Rett syndrome caused diarrhea in about 80% of patients,[^8] a tolerability problem that any future use in other conditions would also face.

As of October 2026, ClinicalTrials.gov lists no active trials of trofinetide for brain injury, concussion or fragile X syndrome, and the only active studies involve Rett syndrome. The IGF-1 fragment strategy continues through [NNZ-2591](/peptides/nnz-2591), a related compound that mimics another IGF-1 breakdown product and is in phase 3 testing for Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
Daybue can legally be prescribed off-label, but there is no evidence that it helps people with fragile X syndrome or brain injury, and its side effects are substantial.

evidence.label: Limited: phase 2 trials with mixed results
evidence.text: The brain injury trial was randomized and reasonably large but missed its efficacy goals,[^3][^4] and the fragile X trial was small, short and exploratory.[^5] Solid evidence exists only for Rett syndrome, the approved use.

faq.q: Why did the brain injury trial fail?
faq.a: The company cited more severe injuries than expected, imbalanced groups and drug levels.[^4] It is also possible the drug does not help human brain injury; many treatments that protect neurons in animals have failed in people.

faq.q: Could trofinetide still help fragile X syndrome?
faq.a: The phase 2 signal was encouraging but preliminary.[^5] Without a larger placebo-controlled trial, its value in fragile X remains unknown.

faq.q: How is trofinetide related to NNZ-2591?
faq.a: Both come from the same IGF-1 fragment research. [NNZ-2591](/peptides/nnz-2591) mimics cyclic glycine-proline, another IGF-1 breakdown product, and is being tested in rare genetic disorders such as Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
